lessons.title: S&P 500, Dow Jones, and Nasdaq 100: Reading the US Indices

children.text: On 6 February 2026, the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed above 50,000 for the first time, jumping 1,206.95 points in a single session. Indian business channels ran the number all evening. But a 1,207-point jump sounds far more dramatic than it was: it was a 2.47% move. And the Dow holds just 30 stocks, weighted in a way no modern index designer would choose. The index that most global fund managers actually track is the S&P 500. The one that decides how your Nasdaq 100 ETF on NSE performs is different again. Three indices, three methods, three different answers to the question "How did the US market do today?"

body.text: An index is a recipe, not a thermometer. Which stocks go in, and how each one is weighted, decides what the index tells you. Know the recipe before you trust the headline.

Never compare index levels across indices. The Dow at 52,573 is not "bigger" than the S&P 500 at 7,657, just as the Sensex is not bigger than the Nifty because its number is higher. Each index started from a different base value in a different year. Only percentage changes can be compared.

markDefs.definition: A weighting method where each stock's weight depends on the market value of shares actually available for public trading, excluding shares locked up with promoters, founders or governments. Nifty 50 and the S&P 500 both use it.

children.text: The S&P 500 is maintained by S&P Dow Jones Indices and covers roughly 500 of the largest US companies, about 80% of the US stock market's value. Each company is weighted by

, exactly like the Nifty 50. The difference is that a committee chooses the members, using published rules plus judgement. Being large is not enough to get in. A company must also be profitable and have been trading publicly for at least 12 months.

Keeps the index focused on large companies

body.text: The S&P 500 is 500 stocks, but it does not behave like 500 equal parts. The top 10 companies, led by Nvidia, Apple, Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, make up close to 40% of the index, far above the long-term average of around 20%. When you buy an S&P 500 fund, a large share of your money is a bet on a handful of US technology giants.

children.text: The Dow Jones: Famous, Old and Oddly Built

markDefs.definition: An index where each stock's weight depends on its share price, not its company size. A $500 stock moves the index ten times as much as a $50 stock, regardless of how valuable each company is.
The number the Dow divides the sum of its 30 share prices by. It is adjusted after stock splits and member changes so the index level does not jump for reasons unrelated to market moves.

children.text: Charles Dow launched his average in 1896, when the easiest calculation was to add up share prices and divide. The Dow still works that way. It is a
of just 30 companies: add the 30 share prices and divide by the

, which is now well below 1. The result: a company's influence depends on its share price, not its size. High-priced stocks such as Goldman Sachs and Caterpillar carry some of the biggest weights, while a far more valuable company with a lower share price barely moves the needle. Members are chosen by a committee to represent the US economy, which is why Amazon joined in 2024 and Nvidia replaced Intel later that year.

body.caption: The Dow's method: add share prices, divide by the divisor

body.title: The small company that moves the index
body.prompt: In the illustrative index above, Stock A rises 10% from $500 to $550 and nothing else changes. By what percentage does the index rise? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: The sum of prices rises from $650 to $700, a $50 increase. $50 ÷ $650 × 100 = 7.69%. The index goes from 216.67 to 233.33 points. Stock A is the smallest company by value, yet a 10% move in it lifts the index 7.69%. If Stock C, the $2 trillion giant, rose 10%, its price would rise just $5 and the index only 0.77%. That is the price-weighting distortion in one example.

children.text: The Nasdaq 100 and the Nasdaq Composite

The Nasdaq 100 holds the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq, including some non-US companies. Banks and insurers are excluded by design, which is why it is so heavily tilted towards technology, communication and consumer companies. It uses a modified market cap weighting that caps the heaviest stocks so no single name dominates completely. The broader Nasdaq Composite includes almost every company listed on Nasdaq, well over 3,000, so it moves in a similar direction but is not the same index. When an Indian news anchor says "the Nasdaq", they usually mean the Composite. When your Motilal Oswal Nasdaq 100 ETF moves, it is tracking the Nasdaq 100.

body.label: SpaceX's fast track into the Nasdaq 100
body.context: Under a fast entry rule effective 1 May 2026, very large new listings can join after 15 trading days instead of waiting at least three months. SpaceX listed on 12 June and joined less than a month later. The S&P 500 kept its 12-month seasoning rule, so SpaceX could not join that index early.

children.text: Concentration is not just a US problem. The Nifty 50 is even more top-heavy than the S&P 500, because it has far fewer stocks and a large banking weight. The top 10 Nifty stocks make up more than half the index, and banks and financials alone are over a third of it.

body.title: One bank, one bad day
body.prompt: HDFC Bank has a Nifty 50 weight of 11.18%. It falls 5% on a disappointing quarterly result while every other Nifty stock is flat. By roughly how much does the Nifty 50 fall, in percent? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Contribution = 11.18% × 5% = 0.1118 × 5% = 0.559%, about 0.56%. On a Nifty level of 25,000, that is roughly 140 points from one stock. It is exactly the same logic as Nvidia or Apple dragging the S&P 500.

children.text: Reading the Headlines Without Getting Fooled

"Dow crashes 800 points" makes a great ticker line. It also misleads. With the Dow above 50,000, an 800-point fall is about 1.5%, an ordinary bad day. Always convert points to percent, and always check all three indices together. If the Nasdaq 100 falls far more than the Dow, the selling is concentrated in technology. If the Dow falls more, look at banks, industrials and high-priced stocks.

body.title: Points to percent
body.prompt: The Dow closed at 52,573.29. The next day, headlines say it "plunged 800 points". What percentage fall is that from 52,573.29? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: 800 ÷ 52,573.29 × 100 = 1.52%. For comparison, the same 1.52% fall on a Nifty at 25,000 would be about 380 points, and nobody would call it a plunge. Points sound scary. Percentages tell the truth.

body.title: Read the split
body.question: One evening, the Nasdaq 100 falls 2.8%, the S&P 500 falls 1.4% and the Dow falls 0.3%. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A broad sell-off hitting every sector equally
Selling concentrated in large technology stocks, while banks, industrials and other Dow members held up
A sharp fall in US bank stocks
A calculation error, since all three indices track the same stocks
body.explanation: The Nasdaq 100 is heavy in technology and excludes financials, so it falls most in a tech sell-off. The S&P 500, with tech giants making up a large chunk of its weight, falls about half as much. The Dow, with only 30 stocks, price weighting and more old-economy names, barely moves. A bank-led sell-off would usually hit the Dow and S&P 500 harder than the Nasdaq 100.

body.title: The Dow's recipe
body.textWithBlank: The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a ___-weighted index, so a stock's influence depends on its share price rather than its company size.
body.explanation: The Dow adds its 30 share prices and divides by the Dow divisor. The S&P 500, Nasdaq 100, Nifty 50 and Sensex all weight companies by market capitalisation instead.

body.title: The morning after a tech sell-off
body.scenario: You wake up at 7:00 am IST and see these overnight US closes: Nasdaq 100 down 3.1%, S&P 500 down 1.9%, Dow down 0.6%. News reports blame disappointing results from a major AI chip company. You hold a Nifty 50 index fund, Infosys shares, units of the Motilal Oswal Nasdaq 100 ETF (MON100) and HDFC Bank shares.
body.prompt: Interpret what happened in the US, then explain how each of your holdings is likely to be affected on NSE today and why.
body.modelAnswer:
What happened: The selling was concentrated in technology. The Nasdaq 100 fell the most because it is dominated by tech and excludes financials. The S&P 500 fell less because tech is a large but not total share. The Dow barely moved because of its old-economy tilt and price weighting.

1. MON100: Hit hardest. It tracks the Nasdaq 100 directly, so expect a fall close to 3.1% at the open, adjusted for any rupee move and the ETF's premium or discount to its NAV.
2. Infosys: Likely weaker. Global tech sentiment is negative, though Infosys sells IT services, not AI chips, so the link is mood rather than direct earnings.
3. Nifty 50 fund: Probably a milder, mood-driven dip. IT is only a modest slice of the Nifty and banks dominate it.
4. HDFC Bank: Least directly affected. Its business is domestic lending. It may slip with the broader market, but there is no link to chip company results.

Before acting, check GIFT Nifty, the Nikkei and Taiwan's market for how Asia is absorbing the chip news, and whether the rupee is moving.

body.title: Your nightly US index check
steps: Note the percentage change, not the points, for the S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq 100.
Compare the three. Is the Nasdaq 100 leading the move up or down? That points to tech.
Check the top five movers in the S&P 500 to see whether a few giants explain most of the move.
If you own MON100 or an S&P 500 fund of fund, compare its last traded price on NSE with its latest NAV.
Ask whether the move reached India through money, earnings or mood before reacting in your own portfolio.

cards.definition: About 500 large US companies weighted by free-float market cap and chosen by a committee. The main benchmark for US equities.
A 30-stock, price-weighted index launched in 1896. Famous, but a poor measure of the overall market.
The 100 largest non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq, using modified market cap weights. Tracked by QQQ in the US and MON100 in India.
A market cap-weighted index of almost every company listed on Nasdaq, well over 3,000 stocks.
An index where higher-priced stocks carry more weight, regardless of company size.
Weighting by the market value of publicly tradable shares. Used by the S&P 500, Nifty 50 and Sensex.
How much of an index's weight sits in its largest stocks. The S&P 500's top 10 are close to 40%; the Nifty 50's top 10 are over 50%.

points: The S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq 100 are built differently, so they can give very different answers on the same day. Compare percentages, never index levels.
The S&P 500 is the main US benchmark: about 500 companies, free-float market cap weighted, with a $22.7 billion size threshold, a profitability test and a committee decision.
The Dow is a 30-stock price-weighted index. High-priced stocks move it most, whatever their company size.
The Nasdaq 100 holds the 100 largest non-financial Nasdaq companies and is heavily tech-tilted. MON100 on NSE tracks it.
SpaceX joined the Nasdaq 100 on 7 July 2026 under a new fast entry rule, while the S&P 500 kept its 12-month seasoning requirement.
Concentration is high in both markets: close to 40% in the S&P 500's top 10 and over 50% in the Nifty 50's top 10.
Convert points to percent before reacting. An 800-point Dow fall from 52,573 is only about 1.52%.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Index levels, weights and eligibility rules are drawn from S&P Dow Jones Indices, Nasdaq, NSE Indices and published market reports as of the dates stated, and may change. The three-stock index is illustrative. Funds and companies named are examples, not recommendations.
